summary:
Guyana remains one of five countries in the Western Hemisphere that criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. Sections 351 to 353 of the Criminal Law (Offences) Act 1893, retained in force after independence, create an offence of gross indecency punishable by up to two years' imprisonment and an offence of buggery punishable by life imprisonment. Prosecutions are rare, but the provisions structure police encounters with LGBT people and anchor public stigma. A constitutional savings clause bars judicial review of laws inherited at independence, which limits the routes by which the remaining statutes can be attacked in court.

There is no legal gender recognition procedure in Guyana. The one direct anti-cross-dressing offence, section 153(1)(xlvii) of the Summary Jurisdiction (Offences) Act, derived from an 1893 statute, was struck down by the Caribbean Court of Justice on 13 November 2018 in McEwan v Attorney General, which held it unconstitutionally vague, archaic and contrary to freedom of expression. The challenge had been filed in 2010 with SASOD after trans women were arrested in 2009 and held for three nights under the provision.

One 2017 case shows what the pre-2018 regime meant in practice. Trans woman Petronella Trotman was stabbed in Georgetown in January 2017, sustaining a neck wound. On 2 March 2017 magistrate Dylon Bess refused her entry to the Georgetown Magistrates Court and told her to dress like a man; the case against her attacker was dismissed. SASOD's Joel Simpson called the magistrate's conduct a dereliction of duty while arguing that Parliament, not the courts, must repeal the 1893 statute.

Rights groups document continuing police abuse of the surviving Summary Jurisdiction clauses. In May 2019 Simpson described officers threatening men found in compromising positions with arrest in order to extract bribes, and harassing same-sex couples at seawalls and parks. People who lodge formal complaints face secondary discrimination at police stations and end up giving watered-down accounts; loitering and vagrancy provisions remain usable against LGBT people, in practice mostly sex workers. Hate crimes often go unreported.

Trans women bear a documented share of the violence. A hearing at the 191st session of the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights in November 2024, requested by the Guyana Equality Forum on the impact of gender-based violence on migrant women, sex workers and transgender women, heard testimony from Blossom Inc., SASOD and the Guyana Sex Work Coalition. The Commission's chair, Roberta Clarke, called on Guyana to take urgent action; the record put to the Commission cited 69 documented cases of violence against trans women between 2018 and 2022.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions do not exist. Discrimination and violence at the hands of law enforcement, religious leaders and others are widespread, and most LGBT Guyanese hide their orientation as a result. A 2022 poll recorded 72% acceptance of LGBT people, with hostility 13 percentage points lower than in 2013.
tangentialFactors:
Five of the six parties contesting the 2025 general election, including the party forming government, backed decriminalisation, which makes the statutory provisions politically contested even while they remain on the books. Public opinion has moved in the same direction, though from a low base: LAPOP's AmericasBarometer acceptance score for Guyana rose from 7.2 in 2010 to 20.6 in 2017 on a 0 to 100 scale, against a regional average of 26.8. A 2013 CADRES survey found 14% support for legalising same-sex marriage.

The violence figures and the police-abuse accounts come from two different pipelines: an international hearing record covering 2018 to 2022 and domestic rights-group documentation from 2017 and 2019. Neither constitutes an official crime statistic, and hate-crime recording is not established in the sources available here.
localsOnly:
Adoption is not barred by sexual orientation or relationship status. The U.S. Department of State reports that LGBT people are not disqualified from adopting and that both married and single people may adopt. In December 2015 the director of Guyana's Childcare and Protection Agency stated that the agency does not discriminate, that no laws bar LGBT individuals or same-sex couples from adopting, fostering or serving as guardians, and that LGBT people should become adoptive parents.

SASOD works with health professionals, with the University of Guyana and with nursing schools across the country to build knowledge about LGBT people, which affects the quality of care residents can obtain. For residents rather than visitors, the practical constraint is under-reporting: formal complaints against police attract secondary discrimination at stations, so accounts given on the record tend to be watered down.
outOfScopeNotes:
Three questions remain unresolved in the sources assembled here. No figure is available for how often sections 351 to 353 are actually prosecuted; the available characterisation is that enforcement is rare. There is no sourced information on whether legal gender recognition reform has been drafted or tabled since the 2018 ruling removed the cross-dressing offence. It is also not established whether the constitutional savings clause blocks every challenge to the 1893 statutes or only some grounds of review.

Whether the cross-party backing for decriminalisation shown in the 2025 election has produced legislative action is not sourced beyond the March 2026 country overview, which still lists the offences as in force. The 69-case figure for violence against trans women comes from the record presented to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights and its methodology is not documented in these sources. No youth-specific or minor-specific findings on health or social care were recorded.
